42	## 2. Approach families
43	
44	**F1. Visual UI-to-code (screenshot or design → code):** si2025benchmarking, xiao2025benchmarking, zhou2025declarui, wu2026looks.
45	- Strengths [I]: real webpages and apps as references [@si2025benchmarking, p. 2; @wu2026looks, p. 3]. Each paper also adds some reliability check:
46	  - visual metrics partly validated against humans [@si2025benchmarking, p. 7];
47	  - a human-calibrated VLM judge with an anchor [@wu2026looks, p. 13];
48	  - navigation measured with app exploration [@zhou2025declarui, p. 7].
49	- Weaknesses [I]:
50	  - Fidelity is mostly visual. si2025benchmarking strips JavaScript [@si2025benchmarking, p. 13].
51	  - Interaction coverage is shallow: navigation edges only [@wu2026looks, p. 5], or element presence as "Implement Rate" [@xiao2025benchmarking, p. 4].
52	  - Structural priors are given as input: a page-relationship description [@wu2026looks, p. 3] or a human-corrected page-transition graph [@zhou2025declarui, p. 4].
53	  - Code quality is unmeasured or measured by proxies or Likert ratings.
54	
55	**F2. Behaviour-observed reconstruction (video, live reference or executable → app):** chen2025iwr†, bai2026recreationworld†, kim2026programdistill†, yang2026programbench†.
56	- This family is the closest match to "AI-assisted reverse engineering" [I].
57	- Strengths [I]: implementation-agnostic behavioural oracles [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 4; @yang2026programbench, p. 5; @kim2026programdistill, p. 4]. The papers also use:
58	  - leakage and isolation controls [@yang2026programbench, p. 18; @kim2026programdistill, p. 10; @bai2026recreationworld, p. 9];
59	  - oracle-quality audits: coverage [@yang2026programbench, p. 7] and interaction-outcome share [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 9].
60	- Weaknesses [I]:
61	  - All four are preprints, and all use single runs.
62	  - Same-family builders appear in yang2026programbench and kim2026programdistill (see Contradiction C10 in the evidence matrix).
63	  - Code quality is measured only through size and structure proxies [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 15; @yang2026programbench, p. 9] or not at all [@kim2026programdistill, p. 6].
64	  - Oracles are coupled to the original's selectors in kim2026programdistill [@kim2026programdistill, p. 35].
65	
66	**F3. Specification-to-app benchmarks with executable oracles:** liu2026benchmarking, lu2025webgen, tran2026vibe, pan2026functional†, zhao2025vibe†.
67	- Strengths [I]: requirement-level executable tests. Several papers check their oracles:
68	  - expert test audits [@liu2026benchmarking, p. 14];
69	  - judge–human alignment [@tran2026vibe, p. 9; @lu2025webgen, p. 9];
70	  - reference-validated tests [@pan2026functional, p. 2];
71	  - upstream human tests with no LLM judge [@zhao2025vibe, p. 5].
72	- Two papers start from existing apps, which brings them close to reconstruction: liu2026benchmarking and pan2026functional [I].
73	- Weaknesses [I]:
74	  - The input is a written specification, not observed behaviour.
75	  - LLM judges and LLM-drafted tests are used (tran2026vibe, lu2025webgen).
76	  - Oracles are thin: about 11 tests per task [@pan2026functional, p. 5].
77	  - Only pan2026functional measures maintainability, through one MI proxy [@pan2026functional, p. 3].
78	
79	**F4. Code-quality studies of LLM or vibe-coded code (static analysis):** molison2025llm, mota2026comparing†, zhu2026understanding, he2026speed (plus the non-functional arm of pan2026functional).
80	- Strengths [I]: established tools (SonarQube, PyExamine), and one quasi-causal design at scale [@he2026speed, p. 7].
81	- Weaknesses [I]:
82	  - The instruments disagree with each other (C3).
83	  - Counts are often not normalised by size [@zhu2026understanding, p. 8].
84	  - Functional correctness is not checked [@mota2026comparing, p. 2], or checked only on 15 samples [@molison2025llm, p. 8].
85	  - Human baselines are weak (competitive-programming submissions) [@molison2025llm, p. 9].
86	  - Tasks are algorithmic snippets, not applications (molison2025llm, zhu2026understanding Exp I).
87	
88	**F5. Human-centred and workflow studies:** borg2026echoes (RCT), mock2026vibe (experiment), asdaque2026novice (mining), fawzy2026vibe (grey review), ehsani2026faster (multivocal review).
89	- Strengths [I]:
90	  - The only randomised maintainability evidence, a hand-off evolution design [@borg2026echoes, p. 13].
91	  - Real developers [@mock2026vibe, p. 16].
92	  - Practitioner definitions of vibe coding [@fawzy2026vibe, p. 1].
93	  - A technical-debt taxonomy [@ehsani2026faster, p. 16].
94	- Weaknesses [I]:
95	  - Small or underpowered samples [@borg2026echoes, p. 19; @mock2026vibe, p. 13].
96	  - Model-generation confound [@mock2026vibe, p. 17].
97	  - Perception or proxy outcomes [@fawzy2026vibe, p. 8; @asdaque2026novice, p. 2].
98	  - Reviews rely heavily on grey sources [@ehsani2026faster, p. 16].
99	  - None studies reconstruction.
100	
101	**F6. Behavioural-specification recovery from running apps:** xiong2026propgen.
102	- Strengths [I]: runtime-grounded property inference with independent annotators (κ 0.81–0.91) [@xiong2026propgen, p. 7]. It is a candidate oracle generator for fidelity testing.
103	- Weaknesses [I]: 12 apps, single run, author-tool overlap in the baselines, and it generates no code.

140	## 4. Contradictions
141	
142	The full entries with both sides, differences and [I] explanations are in `evidence-matrix.md` → "Contradictions". Summary:
143	
144	1. **C1 Maintainability harm.** Project-level warnings and complexity rise after Cursor adoption [@he2026speed, p. 7], but a second developer's effort and CodeHealth show no significant difference [@borg2026echoes, p. 33; @borg2026echoes, p. 38]. Tools, units, scale and time differ, and the he2026speed effect depends on the estimator [@he2026speed, p. 16].
145	2. **C2 Static issues.** LLM code has fewer SonarQube bugs than APPS humans [@molison2025llm, p. 8], vs +30% repository warnings [@he2026speed, p. 7]. The units and baselines differ, so the results are not comparable.
146	3. **C3 Instrument choice.** PyExamine is chosen over SonarQube's "superficial linting" [@zhu2026understanding, p. 2]. Technical-debt tools disagree [@ehsani2026faster, p. 5].
147	4. **C4 Iterative feedback.**
148	   - It hurts non-functional quality without functional gain [@pan2026functional, p. 8].
149	   - It correlates with or enables better outcomes elsewhere [@tran2026vibe, p. 7; @zhou2025declarui, p. 10; @wu2026looks, p. 12].
150	   - The studies differ in feedback type, outcome and design (intervention vs correlation).
151	5. **C5 Looks vs behaves.** chen2025iwr and bai2026recreationworld are only directionally consistent. VFS > IFS is partly built into chen2025iwr's metrics [@chen2025iwr, p. 7]. In bai2026recreationworld the visual channel is below the programmatic one for 9 of 10 models [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 11].
152	6. **C6 MetaGPT.** It nearly always fails in liu2026benchmarking [@liu2026benchmarking, p. 6] but leads on tiny tasks with newer models in mock2026vibe [@mock2026vibe, p. 41].
153	7. **C7 Security.** 87.40% static security [@pan2026functional, p. 6] vs 79.3% of correct solutions failing targeted tests [@zhao2025vibe, p. 6].
154	8. **C8 Code volume.** Rebuilds are smaller than the originals [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 15; @yang2026programbench, p. 9], while assisted development adds code [@he2026speed, p. 8; @borg2026echoes, p. 30].
155	9. **C9 Construct differences.** "Vibe coding" is defined differently in [@fawzy2026vibe, p. 1; @asdaque2026novice, p. 1; @mock2026vibe, p. 15; @he2026speed, p. 4; @ehsani2026faster, p. 17], so these results must not be pooled. The fidelity scores of kim2026programdistill, liu2026benchmarking, lu2025webgen, bai2026recreationworld and chen2025iwr use different oracles and are not comparable.
156	10. **C10 Same-family construction or judging.** The same model family builds or judges the benchmark and then wins in yang2026programbench, tran2026vibe, kim2026programdistill and zhao2025vibe. There is overlap without a visible advantage in liu2026benchmarking, lu2025webgen, bai2026recreationworld, chen2025iwr and wu2026looks. This is untested everywhere [I].

158	## 5. Methodological weaknesses across the field
159	
160	Counts are our tally over the analyses [I]. Each pattern is verified in the cited papers.
161	
162	1. **Single runs, no variance, no significance tests.**
163	   - Main results come from one run or generation per cell, or the number of runs is not reported. Examples: [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 11; @chen2025iwr, p. 8; @kim2026programdistill, p. 12; @lu2025webgen, p. 40; @wu2026looks, p. 9; @yang2026programbench, p. 10; @zhao2025vibe, p. 6; @xiong2026propgen, p. 8].
164	   - Studies that repeat runs: liu2026benchmarking (3 runs) [@liu2026benchmarking, p. 5], pan2026functional (3 runs + 5 reruns) [@pan2026functional, p. 5], and tran2026vibe's 6-app variance panel [@tran2026vibe, p. 8].
165	   - No benchmark paper tests model differences for significance. Where measured, run-to-run variance is large: generation SE up to 5 pp [@tran2026vibe, p. 8].
166	2. **Unvalidated or same-family oracles and judges.**
167	   - Many papers use LLM-drafted tests, LLM-built tasks or LLM judges, often from the evaluated families (C10).
168	   - Judge validation uses raw percent agreement without chance correction [@tran2026vibe, p. 9; @lu2025webgen, p. 9], small or author-labelled panels [@wu2026looks, p. 13], or in-sample calibration [@chen2025iwr, p. 17; @si2025benchmarking, p. 17].
169	   - Some automatic metrics are only declared "consistent" with humans [@xiao2025benchmarking, p. 6].
170	3. **Contamination handling is uneven.**
171	   - Reference apps and programs are popular public projects in most benchmarks.
172	   - Explicit controls appear in only a few: an overlap audit [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 18], no internet plus a language ablation [@yang2026programbench, p. 6], BLEU against the original [@xiao2025benchmarking, p. 5], post-cutoff builds [@xiong2026propgen, p. 11], and keeping task code out of public repositories [@borg2026echoes, p. 66].
173	   - pan2026functional acknowledges exposure [@pan2026functional, p. 2], and its example prompt names the original project [@pan2026functional, p. 3].
174	   - No contamination discussion was found for chen2025iwr, kim2026programdistill, liu2026benchmarking, si2025benchmarking, wu2026looks, zhao2025vibe, molison2025llm or zhu2026understanding (per their analyses) [I].
175	4. **Code quality and maintainability are absent or measured by unvalidated proxies.**
176	   - The proxies used are size and structure [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 15; @yang2026programbench, p. 9], LoC/reuse/dead-component counts [@wu2026looks, p. 4], a single MI index [@pan2026functional, p. 3], Likert ratings [@zhou2025declarui, p. 7], and raw smell counts not normalised by size [@zhu2026understanding, p. 8].
177	   - No reconstruction benchmark combines a behavioural oracle with a validated maintainability measure or a hand-off maintenance task like the one in borg2026echoes [@borg2026echoes, p. 13] [I].
178	5. **Oracle coupling and incompleteness make fidelity scores incomparable.**
179	   - Tests are tied to the original's identifiers: `data-testid` anchors [@liu2026benchmarking, p. 16] and selectors [@kim2026programdistill, p. 35].
180	   - Structural priors are given as input [@wu2026looks, p. 3; @zhou2025declarui, p. 4].
181	   - Suites are thin: about 11 tests per task [@pan2026functional, p. 5].
182	   - Finite suites can only give a lower bound [@yang2026programbench, p. 12; @bai2026recreationworld, p. 22].
183	   - Metrics are partly circular: navigation is scored against the method's own input graph [@zhou2025declarui, p. 7], and VFS uses a different denominator [@chen2025iwr, p. 7].
184	6. **Further recurring problems:**
185	   - No human-developer baseline in any reconstruction or generation benchmark [@yang2026programbench, p. 20; @tran2026vibe, p. 5; @lu2025webgen, p. 7].
186	   - Small human samples [@mock2026vibe, p. 16; @zhou2025declarui, p. 10; @xiao2025benchmarking, p. 11].
187	   - Underpowered RCT [@borg2026echoes, p. 19].
188	   - Internal numeric inconsistencies, flagged in the analyses of borg2026echoes, he2026speed, liu2026benchmarking, molison2025llm, wu2026looks, xiao2025benchmarking, yang2026programbench and zhou2025declarui (see each paper's §9) [I].
189	   - Construct heterogeneity of "vibe coding" (C9).
190	   - Almost exclusively web, Python or CLI targets. Only bai2026recreationworld covers native desktop and Android [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 7]; mobile work uses a web proxy [@wu2026looks, p. 9] or UI-only code [@zhou2025declarui, p. 2].
191	
192	## 6. What this means for our RQs
193	
194	**RQ1 (approaches and their relation to vibe coding).**
195	- Six approach families exist (§2). Inputs range from screenshots, designs, interaction videos and before/after interaction screenshots to live running references, executables plus docs, and natural-language specs [@si2025benchmarking, p. 4; @chen2025iwr, p. 5; @bai2026recreationworld, p. 3; @kim2026programdistill, p. 3; @yang2026programbench, p. 2; @tran2026vibe, p. 3] [V].
196	- Almost all evaluations run autonomous agents or single prompts. Practitioner vibe coding is human-steered natural-language prompting with little review [@fawzy2026vibe, p. 1], and that is studied only in small human experiments [@mock2026vibe, p. 15] or as a field proxy [@he2026speed, p. 4] [I].
197	- Evidence strength: **moderate**. The descriptive picture is consistent, but 7 of 23 papers are preprints and the field moves monthly.
198	
199	**RQ2 (measuring functional fidelity and how well it is achieved).**
200	- Fidelity is measured by four oracle types [I]:
201	  - behavioural test replay (bai2026recreationworld, kim2026programdistill, yang2026programbench, liu2026benchmarking, pan2026functional, zhao2025vibe);
202	  - LLM or agent judges running natural-language tests (lu2025webgen, tran2026vibe, chen2025iwr);
203	  - visual similarity (si2025benchmarking, xiao2025benchmarking, wu2026looks, zhou2025declarui);
204	  - navigation graphs (wu2026looks, zhou2025declarui).
205	- Achieved fidelity is partial everywhere:
206	  - full equivalence is rare [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 11; @yang2026programbench, p. 6];
207	  - the best workflow-level or requirement-level pass rates are about 49–62% [@kim2026programdistill, p. 11; @liu2026benchmarking, p. 6; @tran2026vibe, p. 6];
208	  - interaction logic lags static structure (G-A2).
209	- Evidence strength: **moderate** for "fidelity is far from complete and interaction is the bottleneck". **Weak** for any specific number or cross-benchmark ranking (C9, §3).
210	
211	**RQ3 (code quality and maintainability vs human code).**
212	- The evidence is mixed and does not support a single answer.
213	  - Project-level warnings and complexity rise, but the result is estimator-sensitive and size-driven [@he2026speed, p. 7; @he2026speed, p. 16].
214	  - No short-term downstream maintainability harm was found in an RCT [@borg2026echoes, p. 38].
215	  - LLM code has fewer SonarQube bugs than a weak human baseline, with mixed smells [@molison2025llm, p. 8].
216	  - LLM code shows different smell types [@zhu2026understanding, p. 7].
217	  - Quality is platform-dependent [@mota2026comparing, p. 5].
218	  - Rebuilds are smaller and more monolithic than the originals [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 15; @yang2026programbench, p. 9].
219	  - Practitioners perceive the code as "fast but flawed" [@fawzy2026vibe, p. 8].
220	- No study measures validated maintainability of *reconstructed* applications against their originals [I].
221	- Evidence strength: **weak to moderate** (conflicting results, C1–C3).
222	
223	**RQ4 (methodological strengths and weaknesses).**
224	- Strengths: implementation-agnostic behavioural oracles with leakage controls (F2), oracle audits (coverage, expert κ), judge–human alignment checks, and one preregistered RCT.
225	- Weaknesses: the six patterns in §5.
226	- Evidence strength: **strong** for missing variance and significance testing and for absent maintainability measurement (verified across 12+ papers). **Moderate** for judge, contamination and oracle-coupling problems.
227	
228	**RQ5 (gaps and study design).**
229	- The convergent weak point is the missing joint evaluation of behavioural fidelity *and* validated maintainability for UI- or behaviour-based reconstruction [I]. The partial exceptions are pan2026functional (Python APIs, MI only), wu2026looks (proxies) and zhou2025declarui (Likert).
230	- Candidate gaps for the gap analyst are listed below. **None is claimed as a gap yet: each needs the novelty check in docs/research-standards.md §7.**
231	  1. Joint fidelity + maintainability evaluation of AI-reconstructed apps against their originals, using static quality with size normalisation and more than one tool, plus a hand-off maintenance task as in borg2026echoes.
232	  2. Human-steered vibe-coding reconstruction compared with autonomous agents. All benchmarks are autonomous; future-work statements: [@yang2026programbench, p. 12; @kim2026programdistill, p. 14].
233	  3. Contamination-controlled reconstruction targets, such as post-cutoff, obfuscated or private reference apps (uneven handling, §5.3).
234	  4. Judge and oracle independence: cross-family judges, chance-corrected agreement, and tests of builder- or judge-family self-preference (C10).
235	  5. Whether iterative feedback or self-testing improves fidelity *and* code quality together (C4).
236	  6. Validity of maintainability instruments for AI-generated code: SonarQube vs PyExamine vs CodeHealth vs MI (C3).
237	  7. Black-box oracles that are not coupled to the original's identifiers (§5.5).
238	  8. Native mobile and back-end-inclusive reconstruction.
239	- A design sketch [I]:
240	  - reference apps of known provenance (post-cutoff or private);
241	  - several vibe-coding tools and agents, plus a human-steered arm;
242	  - ≥3 runs per cell;
243	  - a behavioural oracle (trace replay or BDD, black-box selectors) plus a validated visual judge;
244	  - size-normalised static quality from two tools plus a second-developer change task;
245	  - cross-family judges with κ reporting and preregistered tests.
246	- Evidence strength: **weak** (pending novelty check).
247

1	# Methodology comparison: AI-assisted reverse engineering and vibe coding (functional fidelity, code quality, maintainability)
2	
3	Project: 2026-11-11-ai-reverse-engineering-vibe-coding · Date: 2026-11-12 · Basis: 23 complete, full-text, critically reviewed analyses (`papers/*/analysis.md`) and `evidence-matrix.md`.
4	
5	Labels: **[V]** verified in the paper, **[A]** author claim, **[I]** our interpretation. Seven papers are preprints (not peer-reviewed): bai2026recreationworld, chen2025iwr, kim2026programdistill, mota2026comparing, pan2026functional, yang2026programbench, zhao2025vibe. They are marked † below and carry less weight.
6	
7	Terms used:
8	- An *oracle* is the reference that decides whether an output is correct, such as a test suite or a human judge.
9	- *Functional fidelity* means how closely a rebuilt app behaves like the original.
10	- An *LLM judge* is a language model used to score outputs in place of humans.
11	
12	## 1. Overview table
13	
14	All cells are [V] from the analyses unless marked otherwise. "n.r." = not reported.
15	
16	| Paper | Design | Data / sample (N) | Setup | Metrics | Baselines | Statistical testing | Reproducibility |
17	|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
18	| asdaque2026novice [@asdaque2026novice, p. 2] | MSR repository mining (5-page paper) | 22,953 agentic PRs from 1,719 users, AIDev, repos >100 stars | Low- vs high-experience split by commits / account age | Commits and files per PR, acceptance, time to merge, review comments | High-experience users; no non-AI PRs | Mann-Whitney, Chi-square, Benjamini-Hochberg; no effect sizes or CIs; test unit unclear [@asdaque2026novice, p. 4] | Public dataset + replication package [@asdaque2026novice, p. 5] |

(probably 1) | Isolated VMs; Codex or Claude Code scaffolds (model and scaffold confounded) [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 28] | Programmatic accessibility/DOM tests + VLM assertions; LOC, files, largest-file share | Model vs model | No CIs or tests on main scores; bootstrap CIs on secondary analyses [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 12] | Release claimed [A] [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 27]; proprietary models; COI not declared [I] |

31	| pan2026functional† [@pan2026functional, p. 2] | Benchmark | 38 Python repos x 16 LLMs x 3 runs; ~11 functional tests per task [@pan2026functional, p. 5] | Zero-shot single-pass repository generation | Functional pass rate; reference-normalised MI, security, robustness, efficiency, resource | Model vs model; reference as normalisation anchor | None; reruns + rank robustness [@pan2026functional, p. 10] | GitHub [A] [@pan2026functional, p. 11] |
32	| si2025benchmarking [@si2025benchmarking, p. 3] | Benchmark | 484 webpages (+80 HARD); human eval on 100 pages x 5 annotators | Screenshot → single HTML; greedy decoding | Block-Match, Text, Position, Color, CLIP; human win/tie/lose | MLLMs and prompts | Logistic regression validation (79.9%); no model tests [@si2025benchmarking, p. 7] | Release claimed, no URL [@si2025benchmarking, p. 10] |
33	| tran2026vibe [@tran2026vibe, p. 3] | Benchmark | 50 test apps (964 workflows total) x 16 models; 1 generation each [I] | OpenHands-based harness, React/Vite + Supabase | Workflow pass (≥90% substeps) by LLM browser agent; cost; latency | Model vs model | Mean ± SE across apps; variance panel; human alignment [@tran2026vibe, p. 8] | Harness + trajectories released [A] [@tran2026vibe, p. 11] |
34	| wu2026looks [@wu2026looks, p. 3] | Benchmark | 29 apps, 309 screens, 701 nav specs x 6 models = 174 single runs | Screenshots + page-relationship description → React/TS | Build, NavPass, Borda VLM visual, LoC/reuse/dead-component proxies | Model vs model | Wilson CIs for failure sample only [@wu2026looks, p. 8] | Repo + one-command replay [A] [@wu2026looks, p. 10] |
35	| xiao2025benchmarking [@xiao2025benchmarking, p. 3] | Benchmark + user study | 127 pages / 374 interactions x 6 MLLMs x 3 prompts; user study 4 people | Before/after interaction screenshots → one HTML file | CLIP, SSIM, text, Implement Rate; human Usability Rate | Direct prompting | None; human–metric "consistency" claimed only [A] [@xiao2025benchmarking, p. 6] | GitHub [A] [@xiao2025benchmarking, p. 1] |
36	| xiong2026propgen [@xiong2026propgen, p. 7] | Tool + evaluation | 12 Android apps; 985 properties; single run | GPT-5.2 runtime exploration + property synthesis | Functionality / property validity, refinement, new bugs | DroidAgent, naive LLM, 4 bug detectors | Cohen's κ 0.81–0.91 only | Zenodo [A] [@xiong2026propgen, p. 13] |
37	| yang2026programbench† [@yang2026programbench, p. 4] | Benchmark | 200 programs x 9 models = 1,800 runs; 248,853 tests | Execute-only binary + docs, no internet, mini-SWE-agent [@yang2026programbench, p. 5] | % resolved, % almost, % tests passed, structure stats | Model vs model; native test suites for coverage | None; Fleiss' κ for cheating judges [@yang2026programbench, p. 17] | Open-sourced [A] [@yang2026programbench, p. 2] |
38	| zhao2025vibe† [@zhao2025vibe, p. 6] | Benchmark | 186 tasks from 100 Python repos x 12 agent settings; single pass@1 | Agents re-implement a masked feature | FuncPass, SecPass, CWE P/R/F1 | Settings vs each other | None [@zhao2025vibe, p. 8] | GitHub [A] [@zhao2025vibe, p. 1] |
39	| zhou2025declarui [@zhou2025declarui, p. 6] | Technique + comparison + user study | 50 apps (250 pages); ablation 13 apps; 5 developers x 12 apps | CV + MLLM page-transition graph + compile/navigation refinement; human graph correction [@zhou2025declarui, p. 4] | CLIP, SSIM, PCR, CSR, ACIC, AMCT; Likert readability and maintainability | Raw GPT-4o / Claude-3.5 | MWU on non-independent ratings only [@zhou2025declarui, p. 10] | No code or data link (n.r.) |
40	| zhu2026understanding [@zhu2026understanding, p. 4] | Exploratory static analysis (2 experiments) | Exp I: 90 problems x 5 LLMs x 2 prompts + 90 human; Exp II: ~20 MetaGPT apps [I] | PyExamine smell detection | Code / structural / architectural smell counts, LoC | Human solutions (Exp I) | Exp I none; Exp II Spearman / KW without correction [@zhu2026understanding, p. 9] | Zenodo [@zhu2026understanding, p. 10] |
41	
42	## 2. Approach families
43	
44	**F1. Visual UI-to-code (screenshot or design → code):** si2025benchmarking, xiao2025benchmarking, zhou2025declarui, wu2026looks.
45	- Strengths [I]: real webpages and apps as references [@si2025benchmarking, p. 2; @wu2026looks, p. 3]. Each paper also adds some reliability check:
46	  - visual metrics partly validated against humans [@si2025benchmarking, p. 7];
47	  - a human-calibrated VLM judge with an anchor [@wu2026looks, p. 13];
48	  - navigation measured with app exploration [@zhou2025declarui, p. 7].
49	- Weaknesses [I]:
50	  - Fidelity is mostly visual. si2025benchmarking strips JavaScript [@si2025benchmarking, p. 13].
51	  - Interaction coverage is shallow: navigation edges only [@wu2026looks, p. 5], or element presence as "Implement Rate" [@xiao2025benchmarking, p. 4].
52	  - Structural priors are given as input: a page-relationship description [@wu2026looks, p. 3] or a human-corrected page-transition graph [@zhou2025declarui, p. 4].
53	  - Code quality is unmeasured or measured by proxies or Likert ratings.
54	
55	**F2. Behaviour-observed reconstruction (video, live reference or executable → app):** chen2025iwr†, bai2026recreationworld†, kim2026programdistill†, yang2026programbench†.
56	- This family is the closest match to "AI-assisted reverse engineering" [I].
57	- Strengths [I]: implementation-agnostic behavioural oracles [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 4; @yang2026programbench, p. 5; @kim2026programdistill, p. 4]. The papers also use:
58	  - leakage and isolation controls [@yang2026programbench, p. 18; @kim2026programdistill, p. 10; @bai2026recreationworld, p. 9];
59	  - oracle-quality audits: coverage [@yang2026programbench, p. 7] and interaction-outcome share [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 9].
60	- Weaknesses [I]:
61	  - All four are preprints, and all use single runs.
62	  - Same-family builders appear in yang2026programbench and kim2026programdistill (see Contradiction C10 in the evidence matrix).
63	  - Code quality is measured only through size and structure proxies [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 15; @yang2026programbench, p. 9] or not at all [@kim2026programdistill, p. 6].
64	  - Oracles are coupled to the original's selectors in kim2026programdistill [@kim2026programdistill, p. 35].
65	
66	**F3. Specification-to-app benchmarks with executable oracles:** liu2026benchmarking, lu2025webgen, tran2026vibe, pan2026functional†, zhao2025vibe†.
67	- Strengths [I]: requirement-level executable tests. Several papers check their oracles:
68	  - expert test audits [@liu2026benchmarking, p. 14];
69	  - judge–human alignment [@tran2026vibe, p. 9; @lu2025webgen, p. 9];
70	  - reference-validated tests [@pan2026functional, p. 2];
71	  - upstream human tests with no LLM judge [@zhao2025vibe, p. 5].
72	- Two papers start from existing apps, which brings them close to reconstruction: liu2026benchmarking and pan2026functional [I].
73	- Weaknesses [I]:
74	  - The input is a written specification, not observed behaviour.
75	  - LLM judges and LLM-drafted tests are used (tran2026vibe, lu2025webgen).
76	  - Oracles are thin: about 11 tests per task [@pan2026functional, p. 5].
77	  - Only pan2026functional measures maintainability, through one MI proxy [@pan2026functional, p. 3].
78	
79	**F4. Code-quality studies of LLM or vibe-coded code (static analysis):** molison2025llm, mota2026comparing†, zhu2026understanding, he2026speed (plus the non-functional arm of pan2026functional).
80	- Strengths [I]: established tools (SonarQube, PyExamine), and one quasi-causal design at scale [@he2026speed, p. 7].
81	- Weaknesses [I]:
82	  - The instruments disagree with each other (C3).
83	  - Counts are often not normalised by size [@zhu2026understanding, p. 8].
84	  - Functional correctness is not checked [@mota2026comparing, p. 2], or checked only on 15 samples [@molison2025llm, p. 8].
85	  - Human baselines are weak (competitive-programming submissions) [@molison2025llm, p. 9].
86	  - Tasks are algorithmic snippets, not applications (molison2025llm, zhu2026understanding Exp I).
87	
88	**F5. Human-centred and workflow studies:** borg2026echoes (RCT), mock2026vibe (experiment), asdaque2026novice (mining), fawzy2026vibe (grey review), ehsani2026faster (multivocal review).
89	- Strengths [I]:
90	  - The only randomised maintainability evidence, a hand-off evolution design [@borg2026echoes, p. 13].
91	  - Real developers [@mock2026vibe, p. 16].
92	  - Practitioner definitions of vibe coding [@fawzy2026vibe, p. 1].
93	  - A technical-debt taxonomy [@ehsani2026faster, p. 16].
94	- Weaknesses [I]:
95	  - Small or underpowered samples [@borg2026echoes, p. 19; @mock2026vibe, p. 13].
96	  - Model-generation confound [@mock2026vibe, p. 17].
97	  - Perception or proxy outcomes [@fawzy2026vibe, p. 8; @asdaque2026novice, p. 2].
98	  - Reviews rely heavily on grey sources [@ehsani2026faster, p. 16].
99	  - None studies reconstruction.
100	
101	**F6. Behavioural-specification recovery from running apps:** xiong2026propgen.
102	- Strengths [I]: runtime-grounded property inference with independent annotators (κ 0.81–0.91) [@xiong2026propgen, p. 7]. It is a candidate oracle generator for fidelity testing.
103	- Weaknesses [I]: 12 apps, single run, author-tool overlap in the baselines, and it generates no code.
104	
105	## 3. Comparable results
106	
107	**Rule:** numbers are compared only between papers that share the dataset, the metric and the setup. **No pair of papers in this corpus meets all three.** So all cross-paper statements below are directional, not quantitative.
108	
109	| Pair (closest candidates) | What they share | Why the numbers are not comparable |
110	|---|---|---|
111	| si2025benchmarking vs xiao2025benchmarking | C4 validation-set pages, CLIP [@si2025benchmarking, p. 2; @xiao2025benchmarking, p. 2] | Static pages vs interaction regions; different subsets and models; different extra metrics |
112	| zhou2025declarui vs wu2026looks | Multi-screen mobile apps rebuilt from screenshots | PCR (graph edges, scored manually) vs NavPass (Playwright tests); native frameworks vs a React web proxy; different structural inputs |
113	| bai2026recreationworld vs chen2025iwr | A functional channel plus a visual channel | Accessibility tests + VLM assertions vs action replay + OCR/DINO/MLLM; VFS only over reached checkpoints [@chen2025iwr, p. 7] |
114	| lu2025webgen vs tran2026vibe | NL spec → web app; LLM browser judge | Atomic test cases with half credit vs workflows passing at ≥90% of substeps; different model generations |
115	| liu2026benchmarking vs pan2026functional | Rebuild of existing open-source apps against reference-validated tests | Web BDD via Selenium with `data-testid` anchors vs Python pytest on public APIs; different models |
116	| molison2025llm vs zhu2026understanding (Exp I) | Competitive-programming problems vs human solutions | APPS + SonarQube vs CodeContests + PyExamine; different models |
117	| he2026speed vs mota2026comparing | SonarQube issue measures | Change in repository-month totals vs per-KLOC issues in 9 generated apps |
118	| pan2026functional vs zhao2025vibe | Python repositories, test-based correctness, a "security" score | Whole-repo generation + static findings vs feature patch + targeted security tests (C7) |
119	
120	Headline functional-fidelity figures, listed for orientation only. They are **not comparable** because each has a different oracle, input and app type [I]:
121	
122	| Paper | Input → output | Oracle | Best reported |
123	|---|---|---|---|
124	| yang2026programbench† | Executable + docs → CLI program | ~770 behavioural tests per task (median) | 0% resolved; ≥95% of tests on 3% of tasks [@yang2026programbench, p. 6] |
125	| bai2026recreationworld† | Running app → app (5 platforms) | Accessibility/DOM tests + VLM | 58.06% average; 2.8% full programmatic pass [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 11] |
126	| kim2026programdistill† | Live web app → web app | Browser-trace replay | 49.15% cumulative workflows (3 models, 12 apps) [@kim2026programdistill, p. 11] |
127	| chen2025iwr† | Interaction video → single HTML | Agent replay + MLLM assertions | Final 36.35, IFS 24.39 [@chen2025iwr, p. 8] |
128	| liu2026benchmarking | Requirements from existing apps → web app | BDD/Selenium tests | 53.75% Req.Acc [@liu2026benchmarking, p. 6] |
129	| tran2026vibe | NL spec → full-stack web app | LLM browser workflows | 61.77% workflows [@tran2026vibe, p. 6] |
130	| lu2025webgen | NL instruction → website | UI-agent test cases | 27.8% accuracy [@lu2025webgen, p. 8] |
131	| pan2026functional† | Requirements → Python repo | pytest suites | <45% pass rate [@pan2026functional, p. 5] |
132	| zhao2025vibe† | Feature description → patch | Upstream functional tests | 57.0% FuncPass [@zhao2025vibe, p. 7] |
133	| wu2026looks | Screenshots + navigation map → React app | Playwright navigation | 92% NavPass [@wu2026looks, p. 7] |
134	| zhou2025declarui | Screenshots/designs → mobile UI | Manual graph-edge coverage | 96.8% PCR [@zhou2025declarui, p. 9] |
135	
136	Within-paper model rankings are comparable, but single runs make near-ties uninterpretable:
137	- [V] tran2026vibe shows that generation variance dominates evaluator variance (73.5–92.5%) [@tran2026vibe, p. 8].
138	- [I] Rank gaps of a few points in yang2026programbench, wu2026looks, lu2025webgen and zhao2025vibe cannot be separated from noise.
139	
140	## 4. Contradictions
141	
142	The full entries with both sides, differences and [I] explanations are in `evidence-matrix.md` → "Contradictions". Summary:
143	
144	1. **C1 Maintainability harm.** Project-level warnings and complexity rise after Cursor adoption [@he2026speed, p. 7], but a second developer's effort and CodeHealth show no significant difference [@borg2026echoes, p. 33; @borg2026echoes, p. 38]. Tools, units, scale and time differ, and the he2026speed effect depends on the estimator [@he2026speed, p. 16].
145	2. **C2 Static issues.** LLM code has fewer SonarQube bugs than APPS humans [@molison2025llm, p. 8], vs +30% repository warnings [@he2026speed, p. 7]. The units and baselines differ, so the results are not comparable.
146	3. **C3 Instrument choice.** PyExamine is chosen over SonarQube's "superficial linting" [@zhu2026understanding, p. 2]. Technical-debt tools disagree [@ehsani2026faster, p. 5].
147	4. **C4 Iterative feedback.**
148	   - It hurts non-functional quality without functional gain [@pan2026functional, p. 8].
149	   - It correlates with or enables better outcomes elsewhere [@tran2026vibe, p. 7; @zhou2025declarui, p. 10; @wu2026looks, p. 12].
150	   - The studies differ in feedback type, outcome and design (intervention vs correlation).
151	5. **C5 Looks vs behaves.** chen2025iwr and bai2026recreationworld are only directionally consistent. VFS > IFS is partly built into chen2025iwr's metrics [@chen2025iwr, p. 7]. In bai2026recreationworld the visual channel is below the programmatic one for 9 of 10 models [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 11].
152	6. **C6 MetaGPT.** It nearly always fails in liu2026benchmarking [@liu2026benchmarking, p. 6] but leads on tiny tasks with newer models in mock2026vibe [@mock2026vibe, p. 41].
153	7. **C7 Security.** 87.40% static security [@pan2026functional, p. 6] vs 79.3% of correct solutions failing targeted tests [@zhao2025vibe, p. 6].
154	8. **C8 Code volume.** Rebuilds are smaller than the originals [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 15; @yang2026programbench, p. 9], while assisted development adds code [@he2026speed, p. 8; @borg2026echoes, p. 30].
155	9. **C9 Construct differences.** "Vibe coding" is defined differently in [@fawzy2026vibe, p. 1; @asdaque2026novice, p. 1; @mock2026vibe, p. 15; @he2026speed, p. 4; @ehsani2026faster, p. 17], so these results must not be pooled. The fidelity scores of kim2026programdistill, liu2026benchmarking, lu2025webgen, bai2026recreationworld and chen2025iwr use different oracles and are not comparable.
156	10. **C10 Same-family construction or judging.** The same model family builds or judges the benchmark and then wins in yang2026programbench, tran2026vibe, kim2026programdistill and zhao2025vibe. There is overlap without a visible advantage in liu2026benchmarking, lu2025webgen, bai2026recreationworld, chen2025iwr and wu2026looks. This is untested everywhere [I].
157	
158	## 5. Methodological weaknesses across the field
159	
160	Counts are our tally over the analyses [I]. Each pattern is verified in the cited papers.
161	
162	1. **Single runs, no variance, no significance tests.**
163	   - Main results come from one run or generation per cell, or the number of runs is not reported. Examples: [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 11; @chen2025iwr, p. 8; @kim2026programdistill, p. 12; @lu2025webgen, p. 40; @wu2026looks, p. 9; @yang2026programbench, p. 10; @zhao2025vibe, p. 6; @xiong2026propgen, p. 8].
164	   - Studies that repeat runs: liu2026benchmarking (3 runs) [@liu2026benchmarking, p. 5], pan2026functional (3 runs + 5 reruns) [@pan2026functional, p. 5], and tran2026vibe's 6-app variance panel [@tran2026vibe, p. 8].
165	   - No benchmark paper tests model differences for significance. Where measured, run-to-run variance is large: generation SE up to 5 pp [@tran2026vibe, p. 8].
166	2. **Unvalidated or same-family oracles and judges.**
167	   - Many papers use LLM-drafted tests, LLM-built tasks or LLM judges, often from the evaluated families (C10).
168	   - Judge validation uses raw percent agreement without chance correction [@tran2026vibe, p. 9; @lu2025webgen, p. 9], small or author-labelled panels [@wu2026looks, p. 13], or in-sample calibration [@chen2025iwr, p. 17; @si2025benchmarking, p. 17].
169	   - Some automatic metrics are only declared "consistent" with humans [@xiao2025benchmarking, p. 6].
170	3. **Contamination handling is uneven.**
171	   - Reference apps and programs are popular public projects in most benchmarks.
172	   - Explicit controls appear in only a few: an overlap audit [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 18], no internet plus a language ablation [@yang2026programbench, p. 6], BLEU against the original [@xiao2025benchmarking, p. 5], post-cutoff builds [@xiong2026propgen, p. 11], and keeping task code out of public repositories [@borg2026echoes, p. 66].
173	   - pan2026functional acknowledges exposure [@pan2026functional, p. 2], and its example prompt names the original project [@pan2026functional, p. 3].
174	   - No contamination discussion was found for chen2025iwr, kim2026programdistill, liu2026benchmarking, si2025benchmarking, wu2026looks, zhao2025vibe, molison2025llm or zhu2026understanding (per their analyses) [I].
175	4. **Code quality and maintainability are absent or measured by unvalidated proxies.**
176	   - The proxies used are size and structure [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 15; @yang2026programbench, p. 9], LoC/reuse/dead-component counts [@wu2026looks, p. 4], a single MI index [@pan2026functional, p. 3], Likert ratings [@zhou2025declarui, p. 7], and raw smell counts not normalised by size [@zhu2026understanding, p. 8].
177	   - No reconstruction benchmark combines a behavioural oracle with a validated maintainability measure or a hand-off maintenance task like the one in borg2026echoes [@borg2026echoes, p. 13] [I].
178	5. **Oracle coupling and incompleteness make fidelity scores incomparable.**
179	   - Tests are tied to the original's identifiers: `data-testid` anchors [@liu2026benchmarking, p. 16] and selectors [@kim2026programdistill, p. 35].
180	   - Structural priors are given as input [@wu2026looks, p. 3; @zhou2025declarui, p. 4].
181	   - Suites are thin: about 11 tests per task [@pan2026functional, p. 5].
182	   - Finite suites can only give a lower bound [@yang2026programbench, p. 12; @bai2026recreationworld, p. 22].
183	   - Metrics are partly circular: navigation is scored against the method's own input graph [@zhou2025declarui, p. 7], and VFS uses a different denominator [@chen2025iwr, p. 7].
184	6. **Further recurring problems:**
185	   - No human-developer baseline in any reconstruction or generation benchmark [@yang2026programbench, p. 20; @tran2026vibe, p. 5; @lu2025webgen, p. 7].
186	   - Small human samples [@mock2026vibe, p. 16; @zhou2025declarui, p. 10; @xiao2025benchmarking, p. 11].
187	   - Underpowered RCT [@borg2026echoes, p. 19].
188	   - Internal numeric inconsistencies, flagged in the analyses of borg2026echoes, he2026speed, liu2026benchmarking, molison2025llm, wu2026looks, xiao2025benchmarking, yang2026programbench and zhou2025declarui (see each paper's §9) [I].
189	   - Construct heterogeneity of "vibe coding" (C9).
190	   - Almost exclusively web, Python or CLI targets. Only bai2026recreationworld covers native desktop and Android [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 7]; mobile work uses a web proxy [@wu2026looks, p. 9] or UI-only code [@zhou2025declarui, p. 2].
191	
192	## 6. What this means for our RQs
193	
194	**RQ1 (approaches and their relation to vibe coding).**
195	- Six approach families exist (§2). Inputs range from screenshots, designs, interaction videos and before/after interaction screenshots to live running references, executables plus docs, and natural-language specs [@si2025benchmarking, p. 4; @chen2025iwr, p. 5; @bai2026recreationworld, p. 3; @kim2026programdistill, p. 3; @yang2026programbench, p. 2; @tran2026vibe, p. 3] [V].
196	- Almost all evaluations run autonomous agents or single prompts. Practitioner vibe coding is human-steered natural-language prompting with little review [@fawzy2026vibe, p. 1], and that is studied only in small human experiments [@mock2026vibe, p. 15] or as a field proxy [@he2026speed, p. 4] [I].
197	- Evidence strength: **moderate**. The descriptive picture is consistent, but 7 of 23 papers are preprints and the field moves monthly.
198	
199	**RQ2 (measuring functional fidelity and how well it is achieved).**
200	- Fidelity is measured by four oracle types [I]:
201	  - behavioural test replay (bai2026recreationworld, kim2026programdistill, yang2026programbench, liu2026benchmarking, pan2026functional, zhao2025vibe);
202	  - LLM or agent judges running natural-language tests (lu2025webgen, tran2026vibe, chen2025iwr);
203	  - visual similarity (si2025benchmarking, xiao2025benchmarking, wu2026looks, zhou2025declarui);
204	  - navigation graphs (wu2026looks, zhou2025declarui).
205	- Achieved fidelity is partial everywhere:
206	  - full equivalence is rare [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 11; @yang2026programbench, p. 6];
207	  - the best workflow-level or requirement-level pass rates are about 49–62% [@kim2026programdistill, p. 11; @liu2026benchmarking, p. 6; @tran2026vibe, p. 6];
208	  - interaction logic lags static structure (G-A2).
209	- Evidence strength: **moderate** for "fidelity is far from complete and interaction is the bottleneck". **Weak** for any specific number or cross-benchmark ranking (C9, §3).
210	
211	**RQ3 (code quality and maintainability vs human code).**
212	- The evidence is mixed and does not support a single answer.
213	  - Project-level warnings and complexity rise, but the result is estimator-sensitive and size-driven [@he2026speed, p. 7; @he2026speed, p. 16].
214	  - No short-term downstream maintainability harm was found in an RCT [@borg2026echoes, p. 38].
215	  - LLM code has fewer SonarQube bugs than a weak human baseline, with mixed smells [@molison2025llm, p. 8].
216	  - LLM code shows different smell types [@zhu2026understanding, p. 7].
217	  - Quality is platform-dependent [@mota2026comparing, p. 5].
218	  - Rebuilds are smaller and more monolithic than the originals [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 15; @yang2026programbench, p. 9].
219	  - Practitioners perceive the code as "fast but flawed" [@fawzy2026vibe, p. 8].
220	- No study measures validated maintainability of *reconstructed* applications against their originals [I].
221	- Evidence strength: **weak to moderate** (conflicting results, C1–C3).
222	
223	**RQ4 (methodological strengths and weaknesses).**
224	- Strengths: implementation-agnostic behavioural oracles with leakage controls (F2), oracle audits (coverage, expert κ), judge–human alignment checks, and one preregistered RCT.
225	- Weaknesses: the six patterns in §5.
226	- Evidence strength: **strong** for missing variance and significance testing and for absent maintainability measurement (verified across 12+ papers). **Moderate** for judge, contamination and oracle-coupling problems.
227	
228	**RQ5 (gaps and study design).**
229	- The convergent weak point is the missing joint evaluation of behavioural fidelity *and* validated maintainability for UI- or behaviour-based reconstruction [I]. The partial exceptions are pan2026functional (Python APIs, MI only), wu2026looks (proxies) and zhou2025declarui (Likert).
230	- Candidate gaps for the gap analyst are listed below. **None is claimed as a gap yet: each needs the novelty check in docs/research-standards.md §7.**
231	  1. Joint fidelity + maintainability evaluation of AI-reconstructed apps against their originals, using static quality with size normalisation and more than one tool, plus a hand-off maintenance task as in borg2026echoes.
232	  2. Human-steered vibe-coding reconstruction compared with autonomous agents. All benchmarks are autonomous; future-work statements: [@yang2026programbench, p. 12; @kim2026programdistill, p. 14].
233	  3. Contamination-controlled reconstruction targets, such as post-cutoff, obfuscated or private reference apps (uneven handling, §5.3).
234	  4. Judge and oracle independence: cross-family judges, chance-corrected agreement, and tests of builder- or judge-family self-preference (C10).
235	  5. Whether iterative feedback or self-testing improves fidelity *and* code quality together (C4).
236	  6. Validity of maintainability instruments for AI-generated code: SonarQube vs PyExamine vs CodeHealth vs MI (C3).
237	  7. Black-box oracles that are not coupled to the original's identifiers (§5.5).
238	  8. Native mobile and back-end-inclusive reconstruction.
239	- A design sketch [I]:
240	  - reference apps of known provenance (post-cutoff or private);
241	  - several vibe-coding tools and agents, plus a human-steered arm;
242	  - ≥3 runs per cell;
243	  - a behavioural oracle (trace replay or BDD, black-box selectors) plus a validated visual judge;
244	  - size-normalised static quality from two tools plus a second-developer change task;
245	  - cross-family judges with κ reporting and preregistered tests.
246	- Evidence strength: **weak** (pending novelty check).

# RecreationWorld: Scalable and Verifiable Environments for Hybrid Computer-Use Agents

- Authors: Bai, Shuai; Deng, Jiayong; Fan, Sicheng; Fu, Yikun; Gao, Chang; Hu, Xuhao
- Year / venue: 2026, arXiv (preprint)
- DOI: 10.48550/arxiv.2609.22000 · URL: https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22000
- Source text: `fulltext.txt` (page refs = PDF page index). Version read: arXiv v2, 21 Sep 2026 (p. 1). **Preprint, not peer-reviewed.** Industry paper (Alibaba Group, p. 1).

Labels: **[V]** verified in the paper's own data/tables/results · **[A]** author claim · **[I]** our interpretation.
Every [V]/[A] item ends with a page ref `(p. N)`. Write "not reported" when the paper does not say.

## 1. Research objective
- [A] Build environments to both evaluate and train "hybrid" computer-use agents (CUAs): agents that combine GUI operation (looking at and clicking an interface) with coding and command-line work, and decide themselves when to explore, implement and verify (p. 1-2).
- [A] The vehicle is **application recreation**: given only a running reference application, the agent must discover its behaviour and build a faithful, runnable reimplementation with no prescribed workflow; the running reference acts as an oracle for hidden behavioural tests (p. 1, p. 3).
- [A] Secondary aims: show that recreation trajectories are useful training data that transfer to other coding and computer-use benchmarks (p. 3, p. 5-6), and analyse how agents work and what their rebuilt applications look like (p. 11).

## 2. Research questions / hypotheses
- No formal RQs or hypotheses. Implicit questions [I], based on the section structure (p. 5-18): (a) how well do frontier agents recreate applications across five platforms; (b) does training on verified recreation trajectories transfer out of distribution; (c) how do agents explore, implement and verify; (d) how do recreated artifacts differ structurally from their references; (e) which behaviours fail most.

## 3. Methodology
- Research design: [V] Benchmark and environment paper with (i) a held-out benchmark evaluation of ten frontier models, (ii) a supervised fine-tuning (SFT) transfer experiment with two model initialisations, (iii) a paired auxiliary comparison of two tool interfaces, and (iv) descriptive trajectory, artifact and failure analyses plus case studies (p. 5-6, p. 10-20, p. 38-47).
- Approach / model / intervention: [V] Agent gets a task prompt, interactive access to the running reference, and an environment with GUI control and development tools; it returns source that must build and launch (desktop source + build/launch scripts; Android Gradle project -> APK; Web scaffolded source -> self-contained `index.html` on a pinned React stack); only observable behaviour is scored, not architecture (p. 3, p. 7). Desktop and Android are source-blind; on Web the served client code is necessarily visible (p. 7). Each rollout has a 20-hour wall-clock budget (p. 4, p. 28).
- Baselines or comparison conditions: [V] Ten models with their scaffolds: GPT-6 Astra and GPT-5.6 Sol via Codex; Claude Opus 5, Claude Opus 4.8, Gemini 3.7 Flash, Kimi K3, GLM-5.3, Grok 4.6, Qwen3.8-Max-0902 and Qwen3.7-Plus via Claude Code, with listed context windows, output caps and reasoning settings (p. 28). For transfer: each run's first evaluated checkpoint (p. 1, p. 6). [I] No human-developer baseline is reported (checked p. 10-11, p. 28).

## 4. Dataset and sample
- Data source(s): [V] Native references from open-source GitHub repositories (desktop) and GitHub/F-Droid projects (Android), pinned to upstream commits; Web from 44 benchmark-authored synthetic sites and 6 openly licensed real sites (e.g. postgresql.org, webpack.js.org) (p. 7-8, p. 27). Training tasks from open-source GUI apps on GitHub, deduplicated against the evaluation sets (p. 5).
- Sample size (N) and unit: [V] 250 tasks (applications/websites), 50 per platform (p. 7). Median production source of references: Ubuntu 49.3k, macOS 13.5k, Windows 6.7k, Android 15.0k LOC (p. 8). 81 tasks package 393 fixture files (p. 8, p. 34). Training: 35,000 trajectories (7,000 per platform) (p. 5). One example app has 85 rule-based tests and 35 visual assertions (p. 20). [I] Total number of test cases across the suite: not reported (checked p. 8-9, p. 32-34).
- Sampling / selection method: [V] Excluded libraries, frameworks, extensions and apps needing login or remote services; references must run reproducibly; survivors balanced on domain, framework, source size, feature complexity and upstream activity (p. 8, p. 31-32). Android apps with first-run dialogs were patched to remove them (p. 31). Web pages screened by an agent on eight criteria, then human review (p. 32).
- Data availability (public? link?): [A] Benchmark, environments and test suites released via a website, GitHub, Hugging Face and ModelScope (p. 1, p. 27); per-task licence metadata provided (p. 26-27). The PDF shows link labels, not URLs; release not checked by us.

## 5. Experimental setup
- Procedure, settings, hyper-parameters, tools: [V] Task-isolated, versioned VM/container workers per rollout (p. 4); platform actions exposed as direct MCP tool calls (qwen-cua-driver 0.7.3 on desktop, mobile-mcp 0.1.5, Playwright MCP 0.0.79) (p. 5, p. 28). Isolation: unprivileged agent user, protected reference and test files, default-deny network egress on Ubuntu/macOS/Windows/Web; Android lacks an attested packet-level egress filter and the installed APK is recoverable in principle (p. 9-10, p. 36-38). Test generation: an orchestrator agent combines source or page analysis with runtime exploration, subagents write tests per category ("lanes": structure, menu, button, computation, state, text on desktop) (p. 8, p. 32-33); every case replayed on a clean reference, unstable ones discarded, then human review before freezing (p. 8-9). Transfer: SFT of Qwen3.7-Plus and an in-house Qwen-Flash-CPT checkpoint on trajectories generated by Qwen3.8-Max and filtered by rejection sampling on the verifiers (p. 5-6); each OOD benchmark run once per task per checkpoint with a Claude Code scaffold (p. 6, p. 28-29).
- Not reported [I] (checked p. 5-11, p. 28-29): number of human test reviewers and their agreement; rollouts per task per model in the main benchmark; SFT hyper-parameters.
- [I] The main benchmark is probably a single rollout per task. The one-rollout direct-MCP arm of the Windows / Claude Opus 4.8 comparison (Prog 35.05, VLM 31.00; p. 11) reproduces the Table 11 Windows / Claude Opus 4.8 scores exactly (35.05 / 31.00; p. 30). This is not stated explicitly.
- Code availability: [A] Harness, runners, evaluation code and configurations released on GitHub (p. 27); not checked.

## 6. Evaluation metrics
- Metric — what it measures — why chosen:
  - [V] **Programmatic score (Prog)**: fraction of frozen, reference-validated test cases passed, reading exact text, widget state, navigation, persistence or computed values through the platform accessibility/automation API (AT-SPI, AXUIElement, UI Automation, UiAutomator, DOM/ARIA); Web weights checks by specificity (p. 9). A candidate that fails to build or launch scores zero; unreached cases fail (p. 9).
  - [V] **VLM score**: binary verdicts from a Qwen3.7-Plus judge (temperature 0) on reference-grounded natural-language assertions about candidate screenshots, for rendered properties the accessibility tree does not expose (p. 9, p. 32).
  - [V] **Average score** = mean of Prog and VLM; apps macro-averaged within platform, platforms weighted equally (p. 9, p. 11). **Prog >= 90% / = 100%** = share of apps (near-)fully passing (p. 11).
  - [V] Chosen because they are implementation-agnostic: tests depend on observable behaviour, not source similarity, so agents may choose any architecture (p. 4, p. 8).
  - [V] Artifact metrics: production LOC (cloc), file count, largest-file share, UI framework family (p. 15-16, p. 30-31). Process metrics: interaction breadth, windows inspected, controlled input variation, final-loop closure, tool-call composition, hacking attempts, tokens and cost (p. 12-15).
  - [V] Suite coverage audit: 77% of cases leave the start surface, 24% traverse 2+ surfaces, 94.2% check an interaction outcome, 40.7% require an exact value (p. 9).
39:- Baselines or comparison conditions: [V] Ten models with their scaffolds: GPT-6 Astra and GPT-5.6 Sol via Codex; Claude Opus 5, Claude Opus 4.8, Gemini 3.7 Flash, Kimi K3, GLM-5.3, Grok 4.6, Qwen3.8-Max-0902 and Qwen3.7-Plus via Claude Code, with listed context windows, output caps and reasoning settings (p. 28). For transfer: each run's first evaluated checkpoint (p. 1, p. 6). [I] No human-developer baseline is reported (checked p. 10-11, p. 28).
48:- Procedure, settings, hyper-parameters, tools: [V] Task-isolated, versioned VM/container workers per rollout (p. 4); platform actions exposed as direct MCP tool calls (qwen-cua-driver 0.7.3 on desktop, mobile-mcp 0.1.5, Playwright MCP 0.0.79) (p. 5, p. 28). Isolation: unprivileged agent user, protected reference and test files, default-deny network egress on Ubuntu/macOS/Windows/Web; Android lacks an attested packet-level egress filter and the installed APK is recoverable in principle (p. 9-10, p. 36-38). Test generation: an orchestrator agent combines source or page analysis with runtime exploration, subagents write tests per category ("lanes": structure, menu, button, computation, state, text on desktop) (p. 8, p. 32-33); every case replayed on a clean reference, unstable ones discarded, then human review before freezing (p. 8-9). Transfer: SFT of Qwen3.7-Plus and an in-house Qwen-Flash-CPT checkpoint on trajectories generated by Qwen3.8-Max and filtered by rejection sampling on the verifiers (p. 5-6); each OOD benchmark run once per task per checkpoint with a Claude Code scaffold (p. 6, p. 28-29).
56:  - [V] **VLM score**: binary verdicts from a Qwen3.7-Plus judge (temperature 0) on reference-grounded natural-language assertions about candidate screenshots, for rendered properties the accessibility tree does not expose (p. 9, p. 32).
64:1. Recreation is far from solved: GPT-6 Astra leads with 58.19 Prog / 57.92 VLM / 58.06 average, then Claude Opus 5 (44.16) and GPT-5.6 Sol (42.06); Grok 4.6 is fourth (36.73) and Qwen3.7-Plus is lowest (9.15) — [V] (p. 1, p. 11). (Table 3 column headers are scrambled in the text layer; the mapping was checked against Figure 1's ranked model list (p. 1) and word positions in the PDF (p. 11).)
85:- [I] **Conflict of interest not declared.** All authors are from Alibaba (p. 1); the training data are generated by Qwen3.8-Max, the VLM judge is Qwen3.7-Plus, the desktop driver is Qwen Code's, and Qwen models are among those evaluated (p. 5, p. 9, p. 28). No COI statement. Qwen3.7-Plus, which is also the VLM judge (p. 9), is the lowest-scoring evaluated model (VLM 9.12, average 9.15, p. 11). So no favourable self-scoring is visible, but judge self-preference was not tested.
